tips.title: Exo means out of the chemicals
tips.body: **Exo**thermic sends energy **out** to the surroundings, so the thermometer goes **up**. **Endo**thermic takes it **in**, so the thermometer goes **down**. Both words describe the **surroundings**, which is what your thermometer is sitting in.

tips.title: The named examples are the answer
tips.body: Exothermic: **combustion**, **many oxidation reactions**, **neutralisation**. Endothermic: **thermal decomposition**, **citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate**. If a question names a reaction, check this list before reasoning from scratch.

tips.title: Final minus starting, every time
tips.body: Take the change as **final − starting**, never the other way round. A positive answer means the surroundings warmed, so the reaction is **exothermic**; a negative answer means endothermic. Getting the subtraction backwards flips the conclusion as well as the number.

tips.title: Evaluate means decide
tips.body: For an *evaluate* question, give points **both ways** and then **say which wins and when**. The decision and the circumstances are separate marks from the points, and they are the ones most often left on the table.

why.matters:
Energy is conserved, so a reaction that "gives out energy" has not made any. It has **moved** it — out of the chemicals and into everything around them, which is why the beaker gets warm and the thermometer goes up.

Getting that direction straight is most of the topic, because the thermometer is measuring the **surroundings** rather than the reaction. And once it is straight, both words earn their keep: a reaction can be arranged to warm a meal on a hillside or to chill an injured ankle, and neither needs a plug.

examples.title: The hand warmer and the cold pack
examples.body:
Two packets in the same first aid kit, doing opposite things with the same idea. A hand warmer holds iron powder, and what warms your pocket is **rusting** — oxidation, an exothermic reaction, slowed down to last an afternoon.

A cold pack holds a salt and a sachet of water. Break the sachet and the salt dissolves, and dissolving takes in energy: the pack drops below the temperature of the injury it is pressed against. Neither needs electricity. One gives energy out, the other takes it in.

visual.alt: A table comparing a hand warmer, in which iron rusting gives energy out and the surroundings warm up, with a cold pack, in which a salt dissolving takes energy in and the surroundings cool down

examples.title: Why sherbet is cold on your tongue
examples.body:
Sherbet is citric acid and sodium hydrogencarbonate, kept dry in the packet. The moment it meets saliva they react, which is where the fizz comes from — and the reaction is **endothermic**.

It takes in more energy breaking bonds than it gives out making new ones, and the nearest supply is your tongue. So the cooling is not a flavouring or a trick of the mint: it is the surroundings losing energy to a reaction, and your tongue is the surroundings.

examples.title: Is a self-heating can worth it?
examples.body:
A self-heating can warms its own contents with a reaction in the base, usually quicklime and water. Questions about it are marked as **evaluations**, which means weighing both sides and then deciding — not listing features.

It works on a mountain with no power and no fire, and that is worth a great deal to the right person. It is also heavier to carry, more expensive than a flask, usable once, and leaves more to throw away. Which way it comes out depends entirely on where you are standing when you open it.

boxes.body: No fire, no plug, no kettle needed.

boxes.title: Heavy
boxes.body: You carry the reactants as well as the drink.

boxes.title: Once only
boxes.body: The reaction cannot be run backwards.

boxes.title: More waste
boxes.body: A used one weighs the same and does nothing.

steps.title: Energy is conserved, so where does it go?
steps.body:
Start from the rule that never breaks: **energy is conserved**. The amount of energy in the universe at the end of a reaction is exactly the same as before it.

So when a reaction "gives out energy", nothing is created. Energy has simply moved from the chemicals to their **surroundings**, and if a reaction takes energy in, it has moved the other way.

That gives the two words this topic is built on, and both are defined by what happens to the **surroundings**, not to the chemicals.

- An **exothermic** reaction **transfers energy to the surroundings**, so the temperature of the surroundings **increases**.
- An **endothermic** reaction **takes in energy from the surroundings**, so the temperature of the surroundings **decreases**.

A thermometer in the beaker is measuring the surroundings. If the reading goes up, the reaction is exothermic.

One more consequence of conservation: if a reaction transfers energy out, the **products must have less energy than the reactants**, by exactly the amount transferred.

steps.title: Which reactions are which
steps.body:
The specification names examples, and questions ask for them directly. Learn these lists rather than guessing.

**Exothermic** reactions include:

- **combustion**, which is burning
- **many oxidation reactions**
- **neutralisation**, an acid reacting with an alkali

**Endothermic** reactions include:

- **thermal decomposition**, where a compound is broken down by heating
- the reaction of **citric acid and sodium hydrogencarbonate**

The everyday uses are named too, and they follow from the definitions.

- **Self-heating cans** and **hand warmers** use **exothermic** reactions, because they need to give out energy.
- Some **sports injury packs** use **endothermic** reactions, because they need to take energy in and get cold.

Thermal decomposition is the one worth pausing on. It is endothermic because you have to keep heating it: take the heat away and it stops.

steps.title: Required practical 4: temperature changes in reacting solutions
steps.body:
You investigate the **variables that affect temperature changes** in reacting solutions, such as an acid with a metal, an acid with a carbonate, a neutralisation, or a metal displacement.

The method is short, and the marks are in the control.

1. Measure a fixed volume of the first solution into a **polystyrene cup with a lid**, and stand the cup in a beaker so it cannot tip over.
2. Record the **starting temperature**.
3. Add the second solution, **stir**, and record the **highest** (or lowest) temperature reached.
4. Work out the change: final temperature minus starting temperature.
5. **Repeat** and take a **mean**, ignoring any anomalous result.

Why the polystyrene cup with a lid? It **insulates**, so less energy escapes to the room, and the temperature change you measure is closer to the true one.

The variables to control are the **volume** and **concentration** of each solution, and the fact that only one thing is changed at a time.

steps.title: Reading a temperature change
steps.body:
The arithmetic here is deliberately simple, because this part of the specification is **limited to measuring temperature change**. Calculating the energy released, or $\Delta H$, is **not required** in this section.

What you must do is take the change the right way round, and say what it tells you.

steps.note: read the sign, then the meaning

Neutralisation is one of the named exothermic reactions, so this is what we expect

steps.text: The surroundings have **cooled**, so energy has been taken **from** them
This is the named example, and it is the reaction inside a cold pack

check.prompt: A reaction mixture starts at 19.5 °C and finishes at 26.0 °C. What is the temperature change, in °C?
check.solution: Change = final − starting = $26.0 - 19.5 = 6.5$ °C. A positive change means the surroundings warmed, so the reaction is exothermic.

steps.title: Evaluating a use
steps.body:
A common question gives you information about a product and asks you to **evaluate** it. That means weighing the good against the bad and then **reaching a decision**, not simply listing features.

Take a self-heating coffee can. The reaction inside is exothermic.

- **For**: it works anywhere with no power supply, it heats quickly, and the heat is produced where it is needed.
- **Against**: it can only be used once, the chemicals add weight and cost, the temperature cannot be controlled, and the can has to be disposed of afterwards.
- **Decision**: worth it for camping or emergencies, where no kettle is available, but not for everyday use at home where a kettle is cheaper and reusable.

The mark for the decision is separate from the marks for the points, and it is the one most often left unclaimed. Say which way you come down, and say **in what circumstances**, because that is what makes a decision defensible.

steps.title: Your turn: designing the comparison
steps.body:
A student wants to find out whether the **concentration** of an acid affects the temperature rise when it is neutralised by an alkali.

1. Name the independent variable, the dependent variable, and two variables that must be controlled.
2. Describe how the temperature change should be measured.
3. Explain why a polystyrene cup with a lid is used.
4. The student gets rises of 7.5, 7.3, 7.7 and 2.1 °C. Work out a sensible mean and justify what you did with the fourth value.
5. State, with a reason, whether neutralisation is exothermic or endothermic.

Part 4 is worth more than it looks: the mark is for **saying why** you excluded the value, not for the arithmetic.

steps.title: Going deeper: what the thermometer is actually telling you
steps.body:
Two ideas separate a top answer here, and neither needs a calculation.

**First: the thermometer measures the surroundings, not the reaction.** The words *exothermic* and *endothermic* describe the direction energy moves, and the temperature change of the surroundings is the **evidence** for it. An answer that says "the reaction gets hotter, so it is exothermic" has it backwards: the reaction mixture is the surroundings for the chemicals reacting in it, and it is warming because energy has left those chemicals.

**Second: conservation tells you about the products.** If a reaction transfers energy to the surroundings, that energy came from the chemicals, so the **products must have less energy than the reactants**, by exactly the amount transferred. For an endothermic reaction the products end up with **more** energy than the reactants. Nothing is created or destroyed either way.

That second idea is what the reaction profile in the next topic draws as a picture, and what bond energies at Higher tier turn into a number. Here it stays qualitative, because the specification says so: in this section, **calculating energy changes or $\Delta H$ is not required**.

A further subtlety worth having ready. A slow exothermic reaction can feel no warmer than the room, because the energy leaks away to the surroundings about as fast as it is released. It cannot feel **cold**, though: that would need the mixture to drop **below** room temperature, which only an endothermic reaction does. What settles the label is the **direction** of the transfer, measured as a temperature change, not how it feels.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Energy is conserved**: the universe has the same amount before and after a reaction.
- **Exothermic**: transfers energy **to** the surroundings, so their temperature **increases**. Products have **less** energy than reactants.
- **Endothermic**: takes in energy **from** the surroundings, so their temperature **decreases**. Products have **more** energy than reactants.
- Exothermic examples: **combustion**, **many oxidation reactions**, **neutralisation**. Used in **self-heating cans** and **hand warmers**.
- Endothermic examples: **thermal decomposition**, **citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate**. Used in some **sports injury packs**.
- **Required practical 4** investigates the variables that affect temperature change in reacting solutions.
- Use a **polystyrene cup with a lid** to insulate, **stir** before reading, and **repeat** to take a mean.
- Temperature change = **final − starting**. A positive change means exothermic.
- Exclude an **anomalous** result from a mean, and say **why** you excluded it.
- To **evaluate** a use, give points on both sides and then a **decision** with a reason.
- In this section you only measure **temperature change**. Calculating energy changes or $\Delta H$ is **not required** here.

questions.prompt: A student mixes an acid and an alkali in a polystyrene cup and records the temperature rising from 21.0 °C to 28.5 °C. Explain what this shows about the reaction, and explain two features of the apparatus that make the measurement more reliable.
questions.solution: The temperature change is twenty eight point five minus twenty one point zero, which is a rise of seven point five degrees Celsius. Because the temperature of the surroundings has increased, energy has been transferred from the reacting chemicals to the surroundings, so the reaction is exothermic. This is what we would expect, since neutralisation is one of the reactions named as exothermic. The polystyrene cup makes the measurement more reliable because polystyrene is an insulator, so less energy is transferred from the mixture to the room and the measured rise is closer to the true one. Putting a lid on the cup helps for the same reason, by reducing the energy lost to the air above the liquid. Stirring before taking the reading also matters, because it makes sure the thermometer is reading the temperature of the whole mixture rather than one warm spot.

questions.modelAnswer:
**What it shows.** The change is $28.5 - 21.0 = 7.5$ °C, a **rise**. The temperature of the **surroundings** has increased, so energy has been transferred **from the chemicals to the surroundings**: the reaction is **exothermic**. Neutralisation is one of the named exothermic reactions, so this is expected.

**Reliability.** The **polystyrene cup insulates**, so less energy escapes to the room and the measured rise is closer to the true one. A **lid** does the same for the air above the liquid. **Stirring** before reading makes the thermometer read the whole mixture rather than one warm spot.

questions.prompt: Self-heating cans use an exothermic reaction to warm their contents. Evaluate the use of a self-heating can compared with boiling a kettle.
questions.solution: A self-heating can has several advantages. It needs no power supply, so it can be used anywhere, including camping trips and emergencies where there is no electricity. It heats quickly, the heat is produced exactly where it is needed, and no flame is required, which makes it safer in some settings. There are also clear disadvantages. The reaction can only happen once, so the can cannot be reused, while a kettle can be used thousands of times. The chemicals add weight and cost to every can, the final temperature cannot be controlled in the way a kettle can be switched off, and every can used creates waste that has to be disposed of. Weighing these against each other, the self-heating can is worth using where no power supply is available, such as camping or emergency supplies, because in those circumstances the alternative is no hot drink at all. For everyday use at home it is not worth it, because a kettle is cheaper per drink, reusable and produces far less waste.

questions.modelAnswer:
**For.** No power supply is needed, so it works anywhere. It heats quickly, the heat appears where it is needed, and there is no flame.

**Against.** It is **single use**, where a kettle lasts for thousands of uses. The chemicals add **weight and cost** to every can, the temperature **cannot be controlled**, and each can becomes **waste**.

**Decision.** Worth it where there is **no power supply** — camping, or emergency supplies — because the alternative there is no hot drink at all. Not worth it for everyday use at home, where a kettle is cheaper per drink, reusable and produces far less waste.

The decision and the circumstances are separate marks from the points. Listing advantages without deciding caps the score.

examTechnique.body:
Decide first whether the question is about the **direction** of energy transfer, the **practical**, or an **evaluation**, because each wants a different shape of answer.

For direction, always answer in terms of the **surroundings**: exothermic transfers energy to them and warms them, endothermic takes energy from them and cools them. Never write that a reaction creates energy.

For a temperature change, take **final minus starting** and keep the sign. Then say what the sign means before naming the reaction type.

For the practical, the marks are in the reasons: the polystyrene cup **insulates**, the lid reduces loss, stirring makes the thermometer read the whole mixture, and repeats reduce random error. If you exclude an anomaly, say why.

For an evaluation, give points on both sides and then **decide**, naming the circumstances in which your decision holds.

And note the scope: in this section you measure temperature change only. Calculations of energy change belong to the Higher tier bond energy work later.
examinerErrors: Saying a reaction creates energy. Energy is conserved; it is only transferred.
Defining exothermic by the reaction getting hotter rather than by the surroundings warming.
Taking the temperature change as starting minus final, which reverses the conclusion.
Calling thermal decomposition exothermic. It needs continuous heating because it is endothermic.
Saying a polystyrene cup is used because it is cheap, rather than because it insulates.
Excluding an anomalous reading without saying why it was excluded.
Listing advantages and disadvantages in an *evaluate* question without reaching a decision.
Trying to calculate an energy change here. This section is limited to temperature change.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer talks about the surroundings rather than the reaction, so it never says the reaction gets hot and calls that the definition. It reads the sign of the temperature change before naming the type, and it links the direction of transfer to conservation, knowing that an exothermic reaction leaves the products with less energy than the reactants. In the practical it gives the reason for each piece of apparatus rather than naming it, and when it discards an anomaly it says what made the value anomalous. In an evaluation it argues both ways and then commits to a decision, naming the circumstances that make the decision defensible rather than leaving it open.
